intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember or warns you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions with the page covered, and write your own marginal notes beside mine.

sections.title: The Climate System: How It Works
sections.big_idea: Climate is a **30-year pattern**, and the carbon we add stays for centuries, so the **remaining budget** is a finite stock that shrinks every year.
in_plain_words: The climate system has five parts: air, water, life, ice and land. Sunlight warms the surface, and greenhouse gases hold some of that heat in. Without that natural blanket Earth would average −18°C, so the problem is the extra layer humans have added, mainly CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide.

Carbon moves between air, oceans, land and living things. Oceans, forests and soils soak up about half of what we emit, and the rest stays in the atmosphere. Warming also triggers loops such as ice melt and permafrost thaw that add more warming, which is why **each half degree matters more than the last**.

diagram.caption: a positive feedback: the output feeds the next turn

key_terms.meaning: Weather averaged over 30 years or more; the WMO reference period is 1991–2020.
Gases in the air trapping heat, which keeps Earth near +15°C instead of −18°C.
A loop in which warming causes changes that cause more warming.
A threshold beyond which change becomes self-sustaining.
The total CO₂ that can still be emitted before a temperature limit is passed.
Emissions balanced by removals, required globally by mid-century for 1.5°C.

worked_example.title: How long does the 1.5°C budget last?
worked_example.setup: The deck gives a remaining budget of about 170 GtCO₂ and current emissions of about 40 GtCO₂ a year. The second case is an illustrative what-if.
steps: Years left at today's rate: 170 ÷ 40 = 4.25 years.
Counting from January 2026, that lands near the end of 2030, which matches the slide's 'about 2030'.
Illustrative what-if: if yearly emissions were halved to 20, then 170 ÷ 20 = 8.5 years.
Halving emissions doubles the time but the budget still runs out.
worked_example.answer: About 4 years at 40 Gt a year, and 8.5 years if emissions halved.

mistakes: Calling one hot day or one flood 'climate change'. Climate is a 30-year pattern; single events are weather, though attribution science can say how much more likely climate change made them.
Treating the greenhouse effect as the problem. The natural effect keeps Earth habitable; the enhanced effect from human emissions is the problem.
Reading the carbon budget as a flow that resets each year. It is a finite stock, so every tonne emitted reduces what is left.
Assuming the IPCC runs its own experiments. It assesses published research and does none of its own.

recall.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
recall.a: Weather is conditions at a place and time. Climate is the long-term pattern averaged over 30 years or more.

recall.q: Why would Earth average −18°C without greenhouse gases?
recall.a: The natural blanket of gases is what holds heat and lifts the average to +15°C.

recall.q: Name two positive feedbacks.
recall.a: Any two of: ice-albedo, water vapour, permafrost thaw, forest dieback.

recall.q: What does AR6 say about human influence on warming?
recall.a: It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.

recall.q: Roughly how many years of the 1.5°C budget remain at current emissions?
recall.a: About four.

sections.title: The Evidence: What Is Already Changing
sections.big_idea: The signs are already measured: **warming, faster sea rise, heavier rain and heat** are in the record now, and South Asia sits downstream of them.
in_plain_words: Section 2 collects what instruments already show. Temperature is about 1.3°C above pre-industrial, sea level is rising faster each decade, Arctic ice is shrinking and the ocean is more acidic. Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour per degree, so the heaviest rain gets heavier.

For South Asia three systems matter most. Himalayan glaciers feed rivers for 1.9 billion people, the monsoon is becoming more erratic, and humid heat approaches the limit of what a body can handle. **Water, rain and heat** are the three to remember.

left.title: Phase 1: peak water
items: Melt adds river flow now to 2050s
Higher flood risk and glacial lake bursts

key_terms.meaning: Methods that estimate how much more likely climate change made an event.
Warmer water takes up more space, which raises sea level.
Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, a hazard in Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan.
A reading that combines heat and humidity; 35°C is the limit for a healthy adult at rest.
The period when melt temporarily raises river flow before it falls.
Air pollution cooling the land and reducing monsoon rain.

worked_example.title: Turn the rates into amounts
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's rules. Illustrative: take 1.3°C of warming, and the slide's sea level rate of 3.7 mm a year.
steps: More water vapour at 7% per degree: 7 × 1.3 = 9.1 percent.
Sea level in one decade at today's rate: 3.7 × 10 = 37 mm.
Sea level in thirty years at the same rate: 3.7 × 30 = 111 mm.
The slide's 114 mm since 1993 is close to that, because the rate was about 2 mm a year in 1993 and has since risen.
worked_example.answer: About 9.1% more water vapour and 37 mm of sea level a decade.

mistakes: Quoting the sea level rate without saying it is accelerating. The slides give about 2 mm a year in 1993 and 3.7 mm a year in 2006 to 2018.
Saying the monsoon is simply drying. Total rain may change little; the pattern becomes more extreme, with heavy bursts and longer dry spells.
Treating glacier melt as only bad news or only good news. It raises flows for now and cuts them after the 2050s.
Using air temperature alone for heat risk. Wet-bulb temperature includes humidity and sets the survival limit.

recall.q: What are the two causes of sea level rise?
recall.a: Thermal expansion of warming water and melting glaciers and ice sheets.

recall.q: How much more water vapour does 1°C of warming allow?
recall.a: About 7%.

recall.q: What wet-bulb temperature is the theoretical survival limit for a healthy adult at rest?
Why is the Indus especially exposed to glacier loss?
recall.a: It is about 70% glacier-fed, so Pakistan's agriculture depends on it.

recall.q: What did World Weather Attribution find for the 2022 Pakistan floods?
recall.a: Five-day peak rainfall was made up to 50% more intense by climate change.

sections.title: Causes: Emissions, Sources & Actors
sections.big_idea: Who is responsible depends on the lens: **total, per person, cumulative or consumption**. Each gives a different answer, and all four are true.
in_plain_words: Energy and industry, food and land use, and transport produce the emissions. China emits most in total, the US emits most per person, and the US has the largest cumulative share since 1850. India is third in total yet low per person at 1.9 tonnes, and its cumulative share is under 4%.

Accounting rules change the picture again. Counting where goods are made hides where they are consumed, and corporate Scope 3 emissions are often 80–90% of a footprint. Underneath sits a political economy: **fossil fuel subsidies, lobbying and coal states** that depend on the industry.

key_terms.meaning: Total CO₂ added since 1850, which sets the stock in the air today.
Emissions counted where goods are used instead of where they are made.
Value chain emissions beyond a firm's own sites and purchased power.
An investment, such as a coal plant, forced to close before its payback.
Phasing out fossil fuels while protecting workers and communities.
Agriculture, forestry and other land use; about 23% of global GHGs.

worked_example.title: Compare three lenses
worked_example.setup: Use figures from slides 20 and 23, and the food data from slide 25.
steps: US per person against India: 14.9 ÷ 1.9 = 7.84 times.
UK consumption against production: 7.9 ÷ 3.7 = 2.14 times.
The UK consumption extra is 7.9 − 3.7 = 4.2 t per person.
Beef against lentils per kilogram: 99 ÷ 0.9 = 110 times.
worked_example.answer: A US resident emits about 7.8 times an Indian; UK consumption is 2.1 times UK production.

mistakes: Saying India is a top polluter without adding per person and cumulative figures. India is third in total yet emits 1.9 t per person.
Using production figures to judge rich countries. Consumption-based figures roughly double the UK's.
Accepting a net zero claim that covers Scopes 1 and 2 only, when Scope 3 is typically 80–90% of the corporate footprint.
Assuming one person's diet can replace changes in how food is produced. The slide says systemic change is needed.

recall.q: Which country has the largest cumulative share of CO₂ since 1850?
recall.a: The USA, at about 25%.

recall.q: What is India's share of cumulative emissions and of world population?
recall.a: Under 4% of emissions and about 18% of the population.

recall.q: What do Scopes 1, 2 and 3 cover?
recall.a: Direct emissions, purchased electricity and heat, and all other value chain emissions.

recall.q: How many people work directly in coal in India?
recall.a: More than 4 million.

recall.q: What share of global GHG emissions comes from AFOLU?
recall.a: About 23%.

sections.title: Impacts: Global & South Asian
sections.big_idea: Climate impacts **compound on people already on the margin**: farmers, women, fishers and slum residents carry the heaviest load.
in_plain_words: Every system we depend on is affected. Crop yields fall by about 4–6% per degree in India, 54% of districts face high water stress, heat and disease ranges expand, and millions move because of floods and rising seas. The economic case adds up to losses that rise steeply with temperature.

Impacts do not arrive one at a time. A family on the Odisha coast meets heat, cyclones, salt in the fields, fewer fish and more disease together. The slides stress that vulnerability follows class, caste and gender, so **who you are decides what a given climate shock costs you**.

diagram.caption: the convergence problem, as the deck describes it

key_terms.meaning: Demand for water close to or beyond what is reliably available.
Distress caused by environmental change in one's home place.
A phrase with no definition in international law.
The rate that shrinks future damages when valuing them today.
A pressure that intensifies stresses already present, such as conflict over water.
The World Bank study projecting 216M internal climate migrants by 2050.

worked_example.title: Read a yield loss per degree
worked_example.setup: Slide 27 gives a fall of 4 to 6 percent of Indian yield per 1°C. Illustrative: apply it in a straight line to 2°C, for a farm that harvests 3,000 kg.
steps: Low estimate at 2°C: 4 × 2 = 8 percent.
High estimate at 2°C: 6 × 2 = 12 percent.
Kilograms lost, low case: 3,000 × 0.08 = 240 kg.
Kilograms lost, high case: 3,000 × 0.12 = 360 kg.
worked_example.answer: A loss of 8 to 12 percent, or 240 to 360 kg from a 3,000 kg harvest.

mistakes: Quoting the displacement figure on slide 30 without its source. The tile and the text give 32.6M disaster displacements worldwide in 2022 (IDMC).
Describing climate change as a direct cause of conflict. The deck calls it a threat multiplier that adds to existing stress.
Treating Nordhaus's and Stern's results as a technical dispute. The deck says the discount rate is an ethical choice about future generations.
Assessing one impact alone for a household. The compounding of stresses is far more severe than any single one.

recall.q: What share of India's districts face high-to-extreme water stress?
What is the legal status of 'climate refugee'?
recall.a: It has no definition in international law, and the 1951 Refugee Convention does not cover it.

recall.q: Which two economists frame the cost of inaction debate?
recall.a: Nicholas Stern and William Nordhaus.

recall.q: Name three groups the deck says are more vulnerable.
recall.a: Any three of: agricultural workers, coastal fishing communities, children, the elderly and disabled, informal urban settlers.

recall.q: What return does the deck give for each $1 of adaptation spending?
recall.a: $3–4 in avoided losses.

sections.title: Mitigation: Cutting Emissions
sections.big_idea: Clean power is now cheap, so the live questions are **speed, hard-to-abate sectors and the quality of net zero claims**.
in_plain_words: Solar costs fell 90% from 2010 to 2023 and onshore wind fell 69%, so renewables are the cheapest new electricity. Yet capacity additions of 295 GW in 2022 sit well below the roughly 1,000 GW a year the deck says is needed. Money, grids and policy hold things back.

Some sectors cannot simply electrify: steel, cement, aviation, shipping and livestock. For these, and for net zero targets generally, test the claim. **Carbon pricing, offsets, carbon capture and tree planting** each have limits that the slides spell out, and the credible path runs through real emission cuts.

diagram.caption: the deck's five greenwashing checks, in order

key_terms.meaning: Levelised cost of energy, the cost per MWh over a plant's life.
Sectors that need process heat, dense fuels or chemistry that makes CO₂.
A reduction that would not have happened without the carbon payment.
The EU's carbon price at its border on imports of steel, cement and similar goods.
Protecting or restoring ecosystems to store carbon.
India's trading scheme for energy efficiency in large industrial plants.

worked_example.title: Check three headline figures
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's own numbers to see whether the percentages hold.
steps: Solar cost fell from $460 to $44 a MWh: 460 − 44 = 416.
Share of the old cost: 416 ÷ 460 = 0.904, which is the slide's 90%.
Pledged tree planting offsets about 1 Gt of about 40 Gt emitted a year: 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025, or 2.5%.
The maximum credible nature-based contribution is 10 Gt: 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25, or 25%.
worked_example.answer: Solar fell about 90%; pledged trees offset about 2.5% a year, and the ceiling is about 25%.

mistakes: Assuming cheap solar means coal disappears quickly. Contracts, grid stability and the political economy of coal states slow the shift.
Treating carbon capture as a proven main solution. The deck reports costs of 2–3 times projections at a tenth of promised scale.
Accepting carbon neutral claims built on offset purchases while operations stay emission intensive.
Quoting individual footprint tables for India. At 1.9 tCO₂ a person the margin for behaviour change is small.

recall.q: By how much did solar costs fall from 2010 to 2023?
recall.a: About 90%, from $460 to $44 per MWh.

recall.q: What is the difference between a carbon tax and an emissions trading scheme?
recall.a: A tax fixes the price and leaves the quantity open; trading fixes the quantity and leaves the price open.

recall.q: Name two hard-to-abate sectors and one reason for each.
recall.a: For example steel needs coking coal in the chemistry, and cement releases CO₂ when limestone is heated.

recall.q: What price per tonne does the IMF say is needed for Paris goals by 2030?
recall.a: About $75 per tonne of CO₂.

recall.q: What share of mitigation could nature-based solutions provide by 2030?
recall.a: About 30%.

sections.title: Adaptation: Living with Change
sections.big_idea: Adaptation **reduces harm from change that has already happened**, and it is underfunded by a factor of about twelve.
in_plain_words: Even with strong cuts, about 1.3 to 1.4°C of warming has already happened and persists, so people must adapt as well as cut emissions. The deck sorts adaptation into autonomous and planned, and into incremental and transformational. Some limits are soft, such as money and institutions. Others are hard, such as a body that cannot cool.

The slides give working examples: resilient seeds, heat action plans, cool roofs and early warning systems with a 10:1 return. They also show the gap. About $340 billion a year is needed and about $28 billion arrives, because adaptation earns no revenue and **private finance stays away**.

diagram.caption: coastal options, from holding the line to leaving it

key_terms.meaning: Adjusting systems to actual or expected climate change to moderate harm.
Change that communities make without formal policy.
System-level change such as relocating communities or redesigning farming.
A biophysical barrier to adaptation, such as lethal heat or permanent flooding.
Forecasting, risk information, dissemination and response protocols together.
State Action Plan on Climate Change; most lack budget lines and monitoring.

worked_example.title: Size the adaptation gap
worked_example.setup: Slide 50 gives an estimated need of $340 billion a year for developing countries by 2030 and current finance near $28 billion.
steps: The shortfall each year: 340 − 28 = 312 billion dollars.
The need as a multiple of today's flow: 340 ÷ 28 = 12.14 times.
The slide quotes a gap of about 12 times, which matches 12.1.
worked_example.answer: A shortfall of about $312 billion a year, roughly 12 times current finance.

mistakes: Treating adaptation as a substitute for cutting emissions. Both are needed, and adaptation does not stop climate change.
Offering technology alone to smallholders. Credit, markets, extension and social norms are often the binding constraints.
Planning urban adaptation without informal settlements, where 65M+ people have the highest risk and no tenure.
Counting a State Action Plan as delivery. The deck says most are documents with no budget or accountability.

recall.q: Which type of adaptation do the slides say is needed beyond about 2°C?
recall.a: Transformational adaptation.

recall.q: What did the Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan use?
recall.a: Early warning systems, cool shelters and community health worker mobilisation.

recall.q: What are the three coastal strategies?
recall.a: Protect, accommodate or retreat.

recall.q: What return do early warning systems give?
recall.a: About 10:1, per the WMO figure on slide 48.

recall.q: Why is adaptation underfunded compared with mitigation?
recall.a: It rarely generates financial returns, so private finance needs public subsidy and guarantees.

sections.title: Climate Finance & Economics
sections.big_idea: Climate money is **too small, too much debt and too little for adaptation**, so the structure of the system matters as much as the amount.
in_plain_words: Developed countries promised $100 billion a year by 2020 and first met it in 2022, mostly through loans. The new target agreed at COP29 is $300 billion a year by 2035. Only about 5% goes to adaptation, and the Loss and Damage Fund has pledges of $700 million against a need of $400 billion or more.

Tools such as blended finance and green bonds try to draw in private money, but the private money drawn in for adaptation is 1:1 or less. Debt makes it worse, since disasters raise borrowing costs. Finance also carries risk: **physical risk** from climate damage and **transition risk** from moving away from fossil fuels.

key_terms.meaning: New Collective Quantified Goal, the finance target that replaces the $100B.
Public or philanthropic money that cuts risk so private investors join.
Climate harm that cannot be prevented by cutting emissions or by adapting.
Financial damage caused by climate impacts such as floods and heat.
Financial loss from the shift away from fossil fuels.
Framework requiring firms to disclose physical and transition climate risks.

worked_example.title: Size two finance claims
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures. The $50 million public tranche and the mobilisation ratio of 1:5 are illustrative; the 1:1 adaptation ratio and the Loss and Damage numbers come from the slides.
steps: Pledge against need, in billions: 0.7 ÷ 400 = 0.00175, which is 0.175 percent.
A mitigation project at a ratio of 1:5 with $50 million public money: 50 × 5 = 250 million dollars of private money.
An adaptation project at a ratio of 1:1: 50 × 1 = 50 million dollars of private money.
The same public tranche draws five times as much private money in the mitigation case.
worked_example.answer: The pledge covers under 0.2% of the need, and the private money drawn in is five times higher for mitigation in this example.

mistakes: Quoting the $100B as proof of delivery. Most was loans, and developing countries dispute counting market-rate loans.
Assuming private finance will fund adaptation. It rarely earns a return, so it needs public subsidy and guarantees.
Treating Loss and Damage as a technical topic. It implies liability, which is why rich countries resisted it for decades.
Using a green bond label as a guarantee. Verification standards vary, and the EU standard is the strictest.

recall.q: When was the $100B target first officially met?
recall.a: 2022, two years late.

recall.q: What did COP29 agree for the new finance goal?
recall.a: $300B a year in public finance by 2035, with aspirational targets up to $1.3T including private.

recall.q: What are the two kinds of climate risk for financial institutions?
recall.a: Physical risk and transition risk.

recall.q: Name two proposals to ease the debt-climate trap.
recall.a: Any two of: debt-for-climate swaps, pause clauses, SDR reallocation, MDB reform.

recall.q: What ratio of private to public money does blended finance reach for adaptation?
recall.a: About 1:1 or less, against 1:5–10 for mitigation.

sections.title: Global Governance & the UNFCCC
sections.big_idea: The UNFCCC moved from **binding targets to voluntary pledges**, which won every country's participation and lost enforcement.
in_plain_words: The UNFCCC was signed in 1992 and its 198 parties meet at the annual COP. Kyoto set binding targets for rich countries, Copenhagen failed to replace it, and Paris in 2015 let each country set its own NDC under a five-year review. Current pledges lead to about 2.7°C.

Negotiators work in blocs. India sits in the G77, BASIC and the LMDC and argues from CBDR-RC, the principle that responsibilities differ by history and capacity. Article 6 carbon markets need a **corresponding adjustment** so that a reduction sold abroad is not counted twice.

events.what: Kyoto: binding targets for Annex I
Sharm el-Sheikh: Loss and Damage Fund

key_terms.meaning: Nationally Determined Contribution, each country's own climate target.
The five-year review of collective progress; the first ended at COP28.
Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
A seller subtracts a sold reduction from its own accounts.
Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcome, traded under Article 6.2.
Brazil, South Africa, India and China, a coordinating group of emerging economies.

worked_example.title: Why the corresponding adjustment matters
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Country A cuts 20 million tonnes and sells 5 million tonnes of credits to Country B.
steps: With the adjustment, A claims 20 − 5 = 15 million tonnes toward its own NDC.
B claims the 5 million tonnes it bought.
Total claimed: 15 + 5 = 20 million tonnes, which equals the real cut.
Without the adjustment, both claim: 20 + 5 = 25 million tonnes, so 5 million tonnes are counted twice.
worked_example.answer: With the adjustment the claims sum to 20; without it they sum to 25 and overstate the cut.

mistakes: Saying the Paris Agreement has binding national targets. NDC ambition is voluntary and nothing enforces it.
Reading COP28 language as a phase-out. It says 'transition away' from fossil fuels, without an enforcement mechanism.
Assuming voluntary carbon markets follow Article 6. They need no corresponding adjustment, which the deck calls a major gap.
Describing India's COP26 stand as obstruction. The deck frames it as a developmental argument, resting on equity.

recall.q: Which agreement replaced top-down targets with NDCs?
recall.a: The Paris Agreement of 2015.

recall.q: How often is collective progress reviewed under Paris?
recall.a: Every five years through the Global Stocktake.

recall.q: What is Article 6.4?
recall.a: A new UN-supervised carbon market replacing the CDM.

recall.q: Name three groups India negotiates in.
recall.a: G77 plus China, BASIC and the LMDC.

recall.q: What does CBDR-RC mean for India's position?
recall.a: Rich countries should decarbonise first and fastest and finance developing country transitions.

sections.title: Climate Justice & Equity
sections.big_idea: Climate justice asks **who caused it, who suffers and who was heard**, then adds time, gender and indigenous rights to the answer.
in_plain_words: The deck names three injustices: historical, because rich countries built the stock of CO₂; distributional, because impacts fall hardest on those least responsible; and procedural, because the most affected have the least voice. The richest 1% emit more than the bottom 50% combined.

The same logic extends in four directions. Future generations bring cases to court. Women die in disasters 14 times more often than men. Adivasi communities hold knowledge and rights that projects often override. Workers in coal regions need a **just transition**, with real alternatives and funding.

diagram.caption: six lenses that appear in the section

key_terms.meaning: Linking climate change to human rights, equity and social justice.
Free, Prior and Informed Consent for projects affecting indigenous communities.
Traditional Ecological Knowledge held by indigenous and tribal communities.
Moving off fossil fuels while supporting workers and affected regions.
Just Energy Transition Partnership, such as South Africa's $8.5B package.
Climate projects that displace communities without consent.

worked_example.title: Sort statements into dimensions
worked_example.setup: Place each statement under one of the three injustices on slide 64, then do one calculation from slide 65.
steps: 'Wealthy nations' past emissions created today's warming' is historical injustice.
'Floods hit informal settlements hardest' is distributional injustice.
'Affected communities are absent from negotiations' is procedural injustice.
Litigation: 2,000 cases have tripled since 2015, so the 2015 level was about 2,000 ÷ 3 = 666.7 cases.
worked_example.answer: Historical, distributional and procedural, in that order; about 670 cases in 2015.

mistakes: Calling climate change only an environmental issue. The section frames it as rights, development, gender and justice.
Treating youth climate activism in India as representative. Rural youth most affected are less present in the movement.
Reading the Forest Rights Act as fully implemented. The slide says implementation remains incomplete.
Planning a coal phase-down with promises instead of alternatives. A just transition needs reskilling, jobs and protection.

recall.q: Name the three dimensions of climate injustice.
recall.a: Historical, distributional and procedural.

recall.q: What did the Indian Supreme Court recognise in April 2024?
recall.a: A right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change.

recall.q: How many times more likely are women to die in climate disasters?
recall.a: 14 times, per UNDP data across 141 countries.

recall.q: What does FPIC require?
recall.a: Free, prior and informed consent from indigenous communities affected by a project.

recall.q: Does India have a national Just Transition Fund?
recall.a: No. The deck says India has no dedicated fund or framework.

sections.title: India's Climate Story
sections.big_idea: India is both **victim and contributor**, with fast renewable growth and growing coal output on the same page.
in_plain_words: India is the third largest emitter yet emits only 1.9 tonnes per person against a world average of 4.7. It is also ranked sixth among countries most affected by extreme weather in 1993–2022. The 2070 net zero year is defended on equity grounds and contested abroad.

On energy, solar reached 73 GW and wind 44 GW, but coal output also rose because demand grew. Grids, DISCOM finances, land conflict and imported panels slow the shift. **State capacity** decides adaptation outcomes, and Mission LiFE puts the focus on individual behaviour.

diagram.caption: both statements are true at once

key_terms.meaning: State electricity distribution company; the deck calls their finances the bottleneck.
Scheme for solar agricultural pumps.
Rooftop solar scheme with a target of 10 million installations.
National Action Plan on Climate Change, with 8 national missions.
India's demand-side initiative listing 75 individual behaviours.
Power purchase agreement; coal PPAs keep plants running.

worked_example.title: What does 500 GW require?
worked_example.setup: Slide 70 gives 185 GW of renewable capacity now and a 500 GW non-fossil target by 2030, over six years. Slide 22 gives 18 GW of solar added in 2023.
steps: Capacity still to add: 500 − 185 = 315 GW.
Per year over six years: 315 ÷ 6 = 52.5 GW.
Compared with the 2023 solar additions: 52.5 ÷ 18 = 2.92 times.
worked_example.answer: About 52.5 GW a year, nearly three times 2023's solar additions.

mistakes: Calling India's coal stance hypocrisy. The slides describe a real tension between development needs and climate goals.
Assuming renewables are already replacing coal. Coal generation rose in absolute terms through 2023.
Judging adaptation from national plans. Outcomes depend on state capacity: Odisha is a model, Bihar and UP face weak capacity.
Treating Mission LiFE as a full climate plan. It targets individual behaviour while the highest-impact choices belong to wealthy Indians.

recall.q: How does India's per capita emissions compare with the world average?
recall.a: 1.9 tonnes against a global average of 4.7.

recall.q: What is India's net zero target year?
Which scheme is the deck's example of India's most impactful adaptation instrument?
recall.a: MGNREGS.

recall.q: Name two constraints on India's energy transition.
recall.a: Any two of: grid integration, DISCOM finances, land conflict, supply chain risk.

recall.q: Who has the fiscal interest in sustained coal output?
recall.a: The Government of India, through Coal India dividends and royalties.

sections.title: Practitioner Toolkit
sections.big_idea: Start with **exposure and vulnerability**, because vulnerability equals exposure times sensitivity divided by adaptive capacity.
in_plain_words: Mainstreaming climate into a programme runs in five steps: screen for exposure, assess vulnerability, identify entry points, adjust the design and track outcomes. The deck gives screening questions and sector entry points from agriculture and WASH to health and governance.

Vulnerability work uses a formula and free tools such as WRI Aqueduct and the CVCA handbook. Measurement is harder, because success is often a loss that **did not happen**. That needs a comparison group or a baseline, plus hazard data logged beside programme indicators.

diagram.note: raise capacity or lower exposure and sensitivity

key_terms.meaning: Building climate risk into programme design, delivery and evaluation.
Climate Vulnerability and Capacity Analysis, a community-level method.
The nature and degree of hazard a system faces.
Ability to adjust, set by assets, institutions, skills, networks and information.
What would have happened without the programme.
The logic linking activities to outcomes, which climate stress can break.

worked_example.title: Score a village before and after
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scores on a 1 to 5 scale, using the slide 77 formula: exposure 4, sensitivity 3, adaptive capacity 2.
steps: Vulnerability now: 4 × 3 = 12, then 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
A programme raises adaptive capacity from 2 to 4.
Vulnerability after: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
The score fell by 6 − 3 = 3, a halving.
worked_example.answer: Vulnerability falls from 6 to 3 when capacity doubles.

mistakes: Starting with an emissions inventory. For most development practitioners the slide says to start with exposure and vulnerability.
Designing WASH for current conditions. The slides advise using 30-year climate scenarios.
Reading outcome data without separating shocks. Economic and climate shocks look alike, so disaggregate by hazard year.
Counting measures implemented as success. IPCC guidance moves from outputs to outcomes and impact.

recall.q: What are the five mainstreaming steps?
recall.a: Screen for exposure, assess vulnerability, identify entry points, adjust design, track outcomes.

recall.q: Write the vulnerability formula.
recall.a: Exposure × Sensitivity ÷ Adaptive Capacity.

recall.q: Name two free tools for vulnerability work.
recall.a: Any two of: WRI Aqueduct, ND-GAIN Index, IMD district data, CVCA Handbook, NATCOM reports.

recall.q: Why is measuring adaptation hard?
recall.a: Success is often an avoided loss, which needs a counterfactual.

recall.q: Name two resilience indicators from the deck.
recall.a: Any two of: livelihood diversification index, climate information access, asset accumulation, adaptive capacity index, recovery time, subjective vulnerability.

sections.title: Further Reading & Resources
sections.big_idea: The closing section is a **toolbox**: sources to read, data to check, institutions to contact and hard issues to weigh before you act.
in_plain_words: Slides 81 to 85 give reading, data platforms, journals, a glossary and the South Asian institutions. Slides 86 to 96 turn to tensions and topics: green hydrogen, urban heat, geoengineering, communication, geopolitics, litigation, oceans, Pakistan and island states. Slide 97 summarises what is known, uncertain and needed.

Use these slides to check claims as well as to extend them. Several carry figures you can test with a calculator, and the chart slides repeat earlier facts in a different form. A source is only useful if you note its **baseline, year and unit**, because the same quantity can look different on two charts.

diagram.caption: how the final section is organised

key_terms.meaning: Adaptation that raises vulnerability or emissions later, such as AC without a clean grid.
Spraying reflective particles high up to cut incoming sunlight.
Rapid rebound warming if aerosol injection stops suddenly.
Machines that pull CO₂ from the air; a costly backstop today.
Hydrogen made by electrolysis using renewable power.
Small Island Developing States, facing possible submersion.

worked_example.title: Test three claims from the toolbox
worked_example.setup: Use the slides' figures. The cost of $1,000 a tonne and the Mammoth plant size come from slide 89; the renewables target comes from slide 92.
steps: Cost of capturing 1 Gt a year: 1,000,000,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000,000,000 dollars, which is $1 trillion.
Plants the size of Mammoth needed for 1 Gt: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 36,000 = 27,778 plants.
'Triple renewables': 3,400 × 3 = 10,200 GW, while the slide states at least 11,000 GW.
The slide's figure is 11,000 ÷ 3,400 = 3.24 times current capacity, so 'triple' is a little over three times.
worked_example.answer: $1 trillion a year and about 27,800 plants for DAC at 1 Gt; the tripling claim is closer to 3.2 times.

mistakes: Treating geoengineering as a substitute for cutting emissions. The slides call it a last resort with no governance, and aerosol injection could disrupt monsoons.
Mixing temperature numbers across charts without checking the baseline. The area chart uses 1951–1980, while other slides use 1850–1900.
Reading India's 5 million tonne green hydrogen target as a forecast. The slide calls it aspirational and sees competitive hydrogen in 2030–2035.
Opening with global statistics when you talk to affected communities. The slide advises starting from changes they have seen.

recall.q: What is the difference between carbon neutral and net zero?
recall.a: Carbon neutral covers CO₂ only; net zero covers all greenhouse gases.

recall.q: Which Indian ministry is the nodal ministry for the UNFCCC?
recall.a: MoEFCC.

recall.q: Which case produced the first court-ordered emissions cut globally?
recall.a: Urgenda v Netherlands.

recall.q: What share of solar panel manufacturing does China control?
recall.a: 80%, per the IEA 2023 critical minerals report.

recall.q: Why is night-time the dangerous period in an urban heat island?
recall.a: Surfaces re-radiate stored heat, so the body cannot recover from daytime heat stress.

notes.2: Use this agenda as a **route map**. Twelve sections run from the physical science through impacts, solutions, money, politics and fairness, and end with practitioner tools. The title slide and this page both say 104 slides, so use the slide numbers printed here.
notes.4: Keep the test short: **weather is one day, climate is thirty years**. The mood and personality analogy works well with a sceptical audience. Learn the five components too, because later slides on sinks, ice and feedbacks each belong to one of them.
notes.5: Without the natural blanket Earth would sit at −18°C, so the effect itself is helpful. The trouble is **the extra layer humans add**. Read the table by asking two things of each gas: how strong is it, and where does it come from? India's methane sources appear at the bottom.
notes.6: The cycle was roughly balanced before industry, so **the stock grows every year we emit**. About half of each year's emissions go into sinks and half stay in the air. The 1,000 year figure explains why cutting emissions later cannot quickly undo earlier ones.
notes.7: A feedback is a loop where warming causes more warming. Learn each loop as a chain of arrows and you can rebuild it from memory. Most thresholds in the table sit near 1.5°C, which is why the **half degree up to 2°C** carries such weight for South Asia.
notes.8: The IPCC reviews research and runs none of its own, so ask of any claim whether an IPCC report backs it. The key word is **unequivocal**. The practitioner advice here is useful: treat whether climate change is real as settled and spend your time on speed, severity and fairness.
notes.9: Keep three numbers: 1.3°C now, 1.5°C as the Paris limit, 2.7°C if current pledges are fully met. The gap between pledges and the limit is **the policy problem in one line**. The coral and heat figures show why half a degree can separate survival from loss.
notes.10: Think of the budget as **a bank account that only goes down**. About 170 Gt left and about 40 Gt used a year gives roughly four years, a division you can check yourself. Remember overshoot too: nearly all 1.5°C pathways now need carbon removal at scale later.
notes.12: Read the four tiles as **the planet's vital signs**: air temperature, sea level, ice and ocean chemistry. The extreme-events paragraph gives you a rule worth quoting. Each 1°C lets air hold about 7% more water vapour, so heavier rain follows directly from physics.
notes.13: Two things push the sea up: warm water expands and ice melts. Name both when asked. Then note the rate has climbed from about 2 mm a year in 1993 to 3.7 mm in 2006 to 2018. Bangladesh is the slide's anchor case, a very small emitter facing very large exposure.
notes.14: Learn the glacier story as **two phases**. For now melt brings more water and more floods. After the 2050s the ice is gone and dry-season flows fall. A plan that counts on today's river flow is counting on the temporary phase.
notes.15: The headline is distribution. Total rainfall may hold steady while the rain falls in fewer, heavier bursts with longer dry gaps. Use the 2022 Pakistan attribution as your example of how scientists link a particular flood to warming, with a stated percentage.
notes.16: Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity, so it tracks the body's ability to cool itself better than air temperature does. Remember two thresholds: **35°C is the survival limit** and 32°C makes hard outdoor work dangerous. Note who is hit: people who cannot stay indoors.
notes.17: Climate acts as a multiplier on stresses that already exist. Species that have lost habitat cannot shift range as temperatures climb. Group the South Asian examples by what each threatens: crop pollination, fisheries, crops through invasive species, and health through the mosquito range.
notes.18: This is the synthesis for Section 2, so it is a good slide to quote. The text is from the 2023 AR6 Synthesis Report. Take away its last line, **delay is not neutral**: each year of waiting narrows the window and leaves the cost to later decades.
notes.20: Two views, two stories. The sector chart tells you where to cut. The country table splits into total emissions, where China leads, and emissions per person, where the US has 14.9 tonnes against India's 1.9. Keep **both views** ready, since each supports a different negotiating position.
notes.21: The atmosphere remembers. What sets today's CO₂ stock is cumulative emissions since 1850, and that changes who looks responsible. India holds under 4% of it with about 18% of world population. Use this as **the factual base of the climate justice argument**.
notes.22: India is third largest in total and low per person, and both facts hold. The slide adds a third lens, inequality inside India: the top 10% emit about 20 times the bottom 10%. A policy discussion that uses only the national average hides who actually emits.
notes.23: Ask where the goods are used as well as where they are made. The UK example, 3.7 tonnes produced and 7.9 consumed per person, is your proof. In the Scope table, Scope 3 is typically 80–90% of a corporate footprint, so a net zero claim that skips it deserves a question.
notes.24: Two arguments share this slide. The physics is settled and the barrier is political. The Exxon item rests on documents and peer-reviewed history. On India, keep three terms together: stranded assets, stranded jobs and just transition. Each names a different loser.
notes.25: Food is a quarter of emissions, so it belongs next to energy in any plan. Use the data tiles: 99 kg of CO₂e for a kilogram of beef against 0.9 for lentils, about 110 times. The slide's caution matters too: diet choices help, but production systems must change.
notes.27: Agriculture is where climate becomes poverty, since 800 million South Asians live from it. Read the yield tiles as losses **per degree of warming**. Then take the slide's quiet point: higher CO₂ lowers protein, iron and zinc in staple crops, so nutrition can fall where yields hold.
notes.28: Water stress arrives from both ends: supply falls and demand rises. The slide's two poles are Pakistan in 2022 with too much water and Balochistan with too little. The groundwater item is a trap. Farmers who pump more to cope with erratic rain drain the aquifer they depend on.
notes.29: The Lancet Countdown gives the health lens. Sort the five pathways into direct heat, disease spread, undernutrition, disaster damage and air quality. The mental health paragraph links crop loss to farmer suicide risk, a connection the slide says is already visible in NCRB data.
notes.30: Two kinds of displacement appear here: sudden (cyclone, flood) and slow (rising seas, water scarcity). The legal gap is the sharpest point, since 'climate refugee' has no definition and the 1951 Convention does not cover it. The tile and the text now agree on 32.6M disaster displacements in 2022, so quote the figure with its source.
notes.31: Treat Stern and Nordhaus as a debate about **how much we value the future**. The discount rate is the hinge. At 1% damages in 2100 weigh almost as much as today's, and at 5% they barely count. The slide calls this an ethical choice and says most economists now find Nordhaus's rate too high.
notes.32: Exposure, income, power and discrimination stack up. Use the global and women figures as openers, then treat the five groups as a checklist when you design a project. Ask of any intervention which of these five groups it would actually reach.
notes.33: Read 'threat multiplier' literally: climate adds pressure to stresses already present. The Syria and Lake Chad cases trace the chain from drought to displacement to conflict. The slide notes climate contributed alongside repression and marginalisation, and that a security frame can harm migrants.
notes.34: Use this as the one-page revision for Section 4. Read across a row to get the trend, the 2050 projection and who is hit. Then read the paragraph beneath it, because the real danger is **compounding**: the coastal Odisha family faces five stresses at once.
notes.36: Costs fell 90% for solar and 69% for onshore wind, which moves the debate from whether to how fast. The India paragraph holds the second lesson. Solar came in below ₹2/kWh and coal is still dispatched, because contracts, grid concerns and politics also set the pace.
notes.37: The record 295 GW sounds large until you set it beside the 1,000 GW a year the slide says is needed. Note where it places the gap: finance, grids, policy stability and supply chains. Africa's 2% of clean energy investment is the equity point to remember.
notes.38: Learn this as the list of **sectors where electricity is only part of the answer**: steel, cement, aviation, shipping and agriculture. Each row gives a reason. The CCS paragraph and the practitioner box give a usable rule: treat heavy reliance on CCS or offsets as a claim to test.
notes.39: Net zero is a balance, with deep cuts first. The five red flags double as a checklist: a distant date with no 2030 milestones, offset reliance, Scopes 1 and 2 only, CO₂ only, and no third-party verification. Legal status in the country table separates the UK and EU from China and India.
notes.40: A tax fixes the price and lets quantity vary; trading fixes quantity and lets price vary. Hold that pair. Then the gap: Paris needs about $75 a tonne and most schemes charge $3–50. The India items show implicit pricing, and CBAM brings an outside carbon price to Indian exporters.
notes.41: Offsets are a quality problem. Learn the five criteria as a test sheet: additionality, permanence, leakage, measurability and co-benefits. The Verra finding shows why additionality is the hardest to prove. For your own work, ask whether an offset sits beside real emission cuts or replaces them.
notes.42: Keep two ideas apart. Demand-side change could cut emissions 40–70% by 2050, mostly in high-income households. The personal footprint idea was popularised by BP in 2004 to turn attention to individuals. For India at 1.9 tonnes per person, the slide says the lever is systems.
notes.43: Nature-based solutions offer up to 30% of near-term mitigation, but arithmetic sets the limit: pledged tree planting offsets about 1 Gt a year, under 3% of emissions. Hold both numbers. Mangroves, peatlands and agroforestry are the South Asian examples to cite.
notes.45: Mitigation addresses the cause and adaptation the consequences, and the world needs both. Remember the two pairs of types: autonomous or planned, incremental or transformational. Hard limits, such as a body that cannot cool, mark where adaptation stops working.
notes.46: Scan the table's last column, since every row has evidence behind it, from 5–30% better yields for resilient varieties to 20–30% less water with DSR. The 'what's missing' paragraph is the practical lesson: credit, markets, extension and social norms often bind before technology does.
notes.47: Ahmedabad's Heat Action Plan is the proof case: warnings, cool shelters and health workers. Apply the slide's equity test to any urban plan. With 65M+ people in slums lacking tenure, a plan that skips them misses the highest risk. Cool roofs and zoning show cheap and politically hard options side by side.
notes.48: Early warning is the best-value adaptation, with a 10:1 return on the slide. India's cyclone record, from 10,000+ deaths in 1999 to under 100 now, is the success story. The gaps list shows where to work next: the last mile, flash floods and heat alerts.
notes.49: Three strategies: protect, accommodate, retreat. Rank them by cost and by how far each works. The Bangladesh paragraph shows why walls alone cannot serve 30 million people. Mangroves give four benefits in one, and the retreat paragraph tells you who bears the cost.
notes.50: The gap is plain arithmetic on the slide: about $340B needed against about $28B delivered. Adaptation earns no revenue, so private money stays away. For India, State Action Plans are mostly documents with no budget line. Ask of any plan where the money is.
notes.52: Remember the $100B story in three beats: promised in 2009, first met in 2022, and counted generously. The counting dispute, whether market-rate loans are climate finance, is the number to ask about. Then note the new goal: $300B a year in public finance by 2035.
notes.53: Blended finance uses public or philanthropic money to take the first loss so private investors will join. Learn the multiplier claim, $1 for $4–10, then the caveat that adaptation sees 1:1 or less. Green bonds are the other tool here, and third-party verification is the check on them.
notes.54: Loss and damage covers harm that neither emission cuts nor adaptation can prevent, including non-economic loss such as territory and culture. Remember the politics: acknowledging it implies liability. A pledge of $700M against a $400B+ yearly need shows why the slide calls it symbolic.
notes.55: Debt turns a disaster into a lasting setback. Pakistan in 2022 is the case: $30B of damage, an IMF programme, and development spending cut to meet its conditions. Learn the four fixes as a list: swaps, pause clauses, SDR reallocation and bank reform. Each has progress but no scale.
notes.56: Separate two risks. Physical risk is damage from climate itself; transition risk is loss from moving away from fossil fuels. The Indian PPA paragraph shows transition risk landing on state budgets. TCFD and BRSR are the disclosure tools that make both visible.
notes.57: Treat this as the section's glossary. Read the right-hand column as **what to do with each idea**: scrutinise offset quality, ask who bears the residual risk, use disclosure as due diligence. The closing paragraph says structure matters as much as quantity, since grants and loans differ.
notes.59: Read the table as a story: voluntary in 1992, binding at Kyoto in 1997, collapse at Copenhagen in 2009, universal at Paris in 2015. The Copenhagen paragraph explains why Paris chose voluntary NDCs. Participation was gained and enforceability lost. COP28 was the first text to name fossil fuels.
notes.60: Paris works as a ratchet: each country sets its own target and a stocktake reviews the total every five years. Its strength is near-universal participation. Its weakness is that nothing enforces ambition, so current NDCs lead to about 2.7°C. India's three NDC numbers are worth memorising.
notes.61: Article 6 has three parts: 6.2 for bilateral deals, 6.4 for a UN market and 6.8 for non-market cooperation. The idea to keep is **corresponding adjustment**: a seller subtracts what it sells so a cut is counted once. Voluntary markets have no such rule, which the slide calls a major gap.
notes.62: Match each bloc to its main demand. G77, LMDC and BASIC are India's usual groupings, AOSIS pushes 1.5°C hardest and the Umbrella Group resists binding finance. CBDR-RC is the principle behind India's stance: shared responsibility, differentiated by history and capacity.
notes.64: Climate justice has three dimensions, easy to recall as **past, present, voice**: historical, distributional and procedural. Use them as labels when you read any climate policy. Ask who caused the problem, who suffers it and who was at the table. The two data tiles are good openers.
notes.65: The intergenerational problem is about **people with no say**. Because CO₂ lasts for centuries, today's choices set the warming that children born now will live with. The litigation list shows the idea turning into law, and the April 2024 Supreme Court recognition is the item to cite in India.
notes.66: Women are hit harder and are central to the response. The pathways show how: mobility limits, care duties, weak property rights and long water collection. For India the sharpest point is that national climate policies are largely gender-blind. Ask of any programme whether its data is split by gender.
notes.67: Adivasi communities face compounding exposure and hold knowledge that adaptation planning can use. Two things to watch: the Forest Rights Act, where implementation is incomplete, and FPIC, which the slide says renewable projects routinely skip. The slide names the result green colonialism.
notes.68: Just transition means workers and places are supported while an industry shrinks. Read the India points as a gap list: no national fund, a skills and location mismatch between 318,000 solar jobs and 4M+ coal jobs, and powerful coal-state politics. The NGO role at the end shows where you fit.
notes.70: Hold India's ambivalence as a list of true statements: third largest emitter, 1.9 tonnes per person against a world average of 4.7, sixth most affected by extreme weather. The slide asks you to avoid calling this hypocrisy. PM KUSUM and PM Surya Ghar are the domestic schemes to know.
notes.71: The achievement and the constraint share one slide. Solar is 73 GW from near zero in 2010, yet coal generation still rose because demand grew. Learn the four constraints as a set: grid, DISCOM finances, land conflict and imported panels. The slide calls DISCOM reform the central bottleneck.
notes.72: Read this slide in two halves. The first explains India's phase-down position as a developmental argument; the second shows how fixed costs and contracts keep coal running. The deck expects PPA expiry in the 2030s to force retirements if renewables are in place. Coal India's revenue role complicates it.
notes.73: Use the table's last column, **reality check**, as your guide. MGNREGS is called the most impactful adaptation instrument by scale until its repeal, and the bracketed note says the Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act replaced it from 1 July 2026, so confirm current scheme names. The closing point is that state capacity decides outcomes.
notes.74: LiFE is India's demand-side pitch: 75 behaviours across energy, water, food and waste. The critical box matters most for practitioners because it asks who the behaviours target. The high-impact choices belong to wealthy Indians, so use that question on any behaviour-change campaign you evaluate.
notes.76: Mainstreaming means weaving climate risk into a programme's design, monitoring and evaluation. Remember the five steps in order: screen, assess, find entry points, adjust, track. Start with exposure and vulnerability, as the slide advises, and use the screening questions as a checklist on your own work.
notes.77: Vulnerability rises with exposure and sensitivity and falls with adaptive capacity. Memorise the formula, then ask which term your programme can change. The table is a list of free sources, such as Aqueduct and IMD district data, for finding the exposure side for your own district.
notes.78: The hard part of measuring adaptation is the thing that did not happen. You need a comparison group or a baseline prediction of losses. Log hazard events beside programme indicators so you can split results by climate stress, then climb from outputs to outcomes to impact.
notes.79: Treat the eight questions as an oral exam for your own programme. Pick the one you answer least well and fix that first. Question 5 is the subtle one: economic shocks and climate shocks look alike in outcome data, so disaggregate by hazard year.
notes.81: Start with the IPCC summary for policymakers at 40 pages, then pick a book by what you need: economics, politics, justice or history. Each entry carries a one-line purpose, so match the book to your question. The South Asia line lists ICIMOD, CSE and WRI India as regional sources.
notes.82: Bookmark three of these: Climate Watch for NDCs and emissions, Aqueduct for water risk by district and the Global Carbon Project for the carbon budget. ClimateTrace goes down to individual plants. The India line names the official sources: IMD, MoEFCC, CEA, CPCB and NITI Aayog.
notes.83: This is a reading list in two tiers. For plain-language science and policy, the slide names Carbon Brief first. For India, look at Mongabay India and Down to Earth. Check access before you plan around a source, because the slide marks which journals are fully open and which only partly.
notes.84: Ten terms on one page, so cover the right column and test yourself. Two pairs are easy to mix up. Carbon neutral covers CO₂ only while net zero covers all greenhouse gases. Maladaptation is adaptation that raises vulnerability or emissions later, with air conditioning as the slide's example.
notes.85: Use the table to find the right office. MoEFCC leads on the UNFCCC and NAPCC, BEE runs PAT and carbon market rules, MNRE sets renewable policy and IMD supplies forecasts and warnings. ICIMOD is the regional body for mountain research. Match your question to a primary role before you write to anyone.
notes.86: Six tensions, each a pair of goods in conflict, such as mitigation against development or urgency against justice. The slide calls managing the last pair the central political challenge. When you write a position paper, name which side you favour and say what that choice costs.
notes.87: Green hydrogen is India's bet for steel, fertiliser, shipping and aviation. Track the cost gap: $4–6 a kilogram today, $2–3 targeted and grey hydrogen at about $1. The slide's realistic timeline is 2030–2035, so treat the 5 million tonne target as aspirational.
notes.88: Cities run 3–8°C hotter than their surroundings, and night matters most because bodies cannot recover. Sort the responses by type: cool roofs, tree canopy, water bodies and community cooling centres. Dense slums peak because they have no trees, ventilation or cooling access.
notes.89: Geoengineering has two families: reduce incoming sunlight, or remove CO₂. Learn the risks by name: uneven regional effects, termination shock and moral hazard. The DAC arithmetic is the memorable part, since $1,000 a tonne at 1 Gt a year costs $1 trillion annually. No body decides who may deploy.
notes.90: Tailor the message to the audience. Start communities from changes they have seen, officials from their own programme data and planning horizons, donors from the evidence each type prefers, and youth from rights and agency. The closing rule is evidence-based optimism, which avoids both false comfort and despair.
notes.91: Fossil dependence falls and mineral dependence rises. Hold three numbers: China controls 80% of solar manufacturing and 60% of critical mineral processing, and the DRC supplies 70%+ of cobalt. Link them to India's panel imports and to the PLI scheme's reliance on Chinese equipment.
notes.92: A ten-item checklist for what the world must change. Group the items as energy (renewables, efficiency, coal, vehicles), industry (steel, cement), land and food, and money and governance. See the carbon price line: 23% coverage at $5–15 a tonne today against $100+ and 60%+ coverage needed.
notes.93: Four rulings form a ladder: Urgenda, Sharma, KlimaSeniorinnen and MK Ranjitsinh in India. Sharma was overturned on appeal and still set a precedent. The corporate cases lean on documented internal deception. The India paragraph expects more cases on NAPCC delivery and disaster response.
notes.94: The ocean takes 90% of the excess heat and 26% of CO₂, which is why its changes cascade. Keep five stressors in view: heat, acidity, marine heat waves, AMOC slowdown and deoxygenation. The India closing point is the 14 million fishers, who are highly exposed and rarely heard.
notes.95: Pakistan combines low emissions (0.4% cumulative), high exposure and fragile finances. Read the items as a chain: glaciers upstream, the 2022 floods, heat in Jacobabad, farming that depends on the Indus, debt conditions after the floods and political limits on planning. It is the deck's clearest injustice case.
notes.96: For island states the threat is submersion, so policy language carries a different weight. The Tuvalu treaty is the legal novelty: citizens may migrate while statehood is preserved without territory. Nearer home, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar islands face similar risks with weaker links to mainland governance.
notes.97: Use this as the course's closing summary and learn its three lists: what is known with high confidence, what stays uncertain and what must be done. The uncertainty list covers timing, regional detail, removal technology and politics. Write your own version of the last list for your programme.
notes.98: The Sankey chart follows CO₂ from energy carrier to sector, left to right. Coal flows into electricity and heavy industry, and transport runs almost entirely on oil. Use that geometry to pick the right decarbonisation path for each sector, remembering that cement and steel emissions are mostly process emissions.
notes.99: The post-1980 acceleration is the part of this chart to remember, and the slide adds that each of the last ten years was warmer than any year before 2010. Check the baseline too. This chart uses 1951–1980, while earlier slides used 1850–1900, so do not mix numbers across charts.
notes.100: A list of next courses. Match them to your gap: development economics for markets and growth, MEL for tracking results, data visualisation for communicating, AI for responsible tools, and the Gandhi and Politics of Aspiration courses for ideas and power. The slide says all are free.
notes.101: Three libraries are named: DevDiscourses with 500+ papers, ImpactLex with 490+ terms and FieldCases with 208 case studies. The six papers listed are the ones this deck cites, so read Burke and colleagues for the economics and Myers and colleagues for the nutrition findings.
notes.102: The US emits about 7 times more CO₂ per person than India, the asymmetry that grounds climate justice. Compare slide 20, which gives 14.9 and 1.9 tonnes for 2022, a ratio nearer 7.8. Different sources and years give slightly different ratios, so quote one source and its year.
notes.103: India's coal share of installed capacity is about 50%, while renewables rose from about 10 GW to over 130 GW in 14 years. Compare slide 70, which gives 185 GW including large hydro. The slide's own conclusion is that the transition is real and the pace must accelerate.
